chapter_theme: Kurinji of the secret love in Kanimedaviyar's quatrains: the hunter's pretext question at the millet field and his confession of it (1, 8, 9), the girl seen on the platform (3, 4), the friend forbidding the night path for its elephants, tigers, snakes and gods (6, 7, 10, 11, 13), the ripening millet that ends the meetings (5), the friend's disclosure of the elephant and flood rescues to the household (2, 12, 14), her plea against a bride price (15), and the lover's madal (16).

1.reading: The man asks the long-haired girls, whose bright faces are like lotuses facing the crescent moon, whether they have not seen an arrow-struck deer come this way into the millet field sown in good time with the first rain on a slope cleared of fragrant sandal.
1.nuance: The question about the wounded deer is the conventional pretext of the hunter who comes to the field; the praise packed into the address (crescent brow over lotus face) shows that the real question is not about the deer. The plural address (தாழ்குழலீர்) takes in the heroine and her friend together.

thinai_evidence.note: a millet field cut out of sandal forest is the kurinji clearing

comparisons.tenor: the girls' faces under brows like the crescent

2.reading: The friend says there is a man who gathered sulli, pool lilies, sobhalika and asoka flowers, sorted them and set them on the girl's hair, and who with a blunt arrow drove off the wet-musth elephant that the shouts from the platform could not turn away.
2.nuance: Two acts make the claim: he dressed her hair, which only a husband or one who means to be one does, and he saved her from the elephant. Said to the household, it is the friend's disclosure of the secret love (அறத்தொடு நிற்றல்), and the bare 'there is one' (உளன்) leaves the elders to ask who.

thinai_evidence.note: pool lilies, the field platform and the wild elephant are kurinji things

3.reading: On the slope where sandal trees were cut down and the ground ploughed for small millet, on the platform built of the cut sandal, the girl like a dark peacock, fragrant with sandal paste, scares off the parrots, and her shouts ring until the parrots cry out.
3.nuance: The word சாந்தம் comes three times with three senses: the felled tree, the platform built from it, and the paste on her body, so the field's whole history is carried on her skin. Line 4 is hard: whether the parrots cry out or the girl's cry is meant is not certain.

thinai_evidence.note: the millet slope and the parrot-scaring girl are kurinji

4.reading: The man says he cannot see her, who is like the Koodal of Maran of unswerving fame, even among the greens of the field, and wonders whether the hair of her with a waist like a slender branch has gone into the vessels of kings whose dark killing spears never fail in battle.
4.nuance: The kings of line 3 may be rival suitors who have come with gifts for her, so that her not being seen means she is being given elsewhere; the Pandya's city as the measure of her beauty brings puram fame into the field.

thinai_evidence.note: the poem gives no land beyond the field greens; the book's heading places it in kurinji

5.reading: The friend tells the peacock-like girl of dark wide eyes that the millet in the plots has ripened before long, as wealth ripens when deeds ripen, and bids her see how this parts them as a hand jerks back from fire.
5.nuance: Comparing the ripening millet to the ripening of past deeds into wealth makes the harvest a fate no one can hurry or delay: the end of the field-watch, and so of the meetings, arrives on its own schedule. Line 2 (பனைவிளைவு) and the fire image of line 4 are hard to fix.

thinai_evidence.note: the ripening millet in its plots is the kurinji field's clock

comparisons.tenor: the millet ripening in its plots
the lovers parted by the harvest

6.reading: The friend bids the lord of the great dark hill, where the waterfall looks like the hill spitting out a fine blue cloth, to listen and judge for himself whether she of spear-sharp eyes that put the blue lily to shame can be at ease while he comes through the thick dark.
6.nuance: The friend puts the judgement on him (நீ ஆய்): the danger of the dark path is argued through her fear for him, not his own. The repeated மானீல / மாநீலம் plays the blue of the hill against the blue of the lily her eyes outdo. ஆயுமோ is read as 'will she be at ease'.

thinai_evidence.note: the great hill and the night visit mark kurinji's midnight tryst

7.reading: The friend tells the lord of the good hill, on whose flowered pepper slopes the long tiger prowls the path watching the elephant, that if he comes by night the daughter of the lord of the good hill will not live.
7.nuance: The same phrase நன்மலை நாட(ன்) names the lover in line 3 and the girl's father in line 4, setting the two men side by side as equals: the night visit endangers a match that could be made openly. The tiger lying in wait on the path carries the danger as a mood; it does no act of a person of the love, so it is scene, not iraicchi.

thinai_evidence.note: pepper slopes, tiger and elephant are kurinji things

8.reading: Looking at the girls at the fields, the man says that one guards the mountain rice and this one the red millet, and wonders whether the love god has given this one his five arrows twice over: what else could it be, when Kaman's arrows are in her eyes.
8.nuance: The count is the joke: Kaman has five arrows, and she, with two eyes, seems to carry ten. Line 3 is obscure and the sense of 'five twice' is a reading.

thinai_evidence.note: mountain rice and red millet fields are kurinji

9.reading: The man says he went alone and unprotected, asking after a beast in a way that was nothing but a ruse, and the girl of flowered hair who took his heart with her beauty, that day among her good companions, took his strength and took its place.
9.nuance: The hero names his own pretext as deceit (வஞ்சமே), and the trickster is the one caught: he went to take and was taken. Line 4 (வலங்கொண்டாள் கொண்டாள் இடம்) may also be a play on right and left, she who went round him to the right took the left, his heart's side.

thinai_evidence.note: the hunter's pretext at the field belongs to kurinji's first meeting

10.reading: The friend tells the lord of the hill, where the pregnant female monkey with black fingers, red face and white teeth scatters the green pool's water with her thick fingers and reaches for the honey dripping on the great rock, not to come by the path where the sky gods roam.
10.nuance: The monkey's sprinkling of water and raising of hands toward the honey look like worship at a sacred hill, which prepares the closing danger of divine beings on the path. A pregnant creature craving honey may hint at the household he should give her, but it fails the act condition for iraicchi, so it stays scene.

thinai_evidence.note: the hill monkey, the pool and the rock honey are kurinji

11.reading: The friend tells the lord of the rich, open hill of rocky falls that, strong as he is with his mighty bow and coming alone, the paths by night are very hard to travel, and he must not come where the musth-streaming elephant meets him.
11.nuance: She grants his strength before refusing him: the bow does not answer the danger, because he comes alone (ஒரு நீ). கரவில் 'without hiding' may glance at the secrecy he keeps, set against his open hill.

thinai_evidence.note: rocky falls, night paths and the wild elephant are kurinji

12.reading: The friend says: let the diviner go, set the kid free, give the toddy to the children; by her nature the blameless girl will not offer her shoulders, round as the tall palm, to anyone but the man who swam the fierce flood and set her on the bank.
12.nuance: The friend stops the rite by naming its true cause: the girl is not possessed but promised, by her own choice, to the man who saved her from the flood. The rescue gives the claim its warrant before the household. பனை is probably பணை (bamboo), the usual vehicle for shoulders.

thinai_evidence.note: the diviner's rite with the kid is kurinji's veri

13.reading: The friend tells the man that their little village lies inside the hills that crowd round it on every side as if they were one hill, and that within those hills are five-hooded snakes and, all around, a forest where elephants gather.
13.nuance: Read as 'snake' and 'elephant' (ஐவாய் நாகம், கைவாய் நாகம்), the two closing lines set a creature that strikes inside the hills against one that roams outside them, so every way in is guarded. The reading depends on emending நாதும் to நாகும்.

thinai_evidence.note: a hill-ringed village in the forest is kurinji

comparisons.tenor: the many hills ringing the village

14.reading: The friend says that when the girl and she were sitting high on the platform in the rich hill of jackfruit and a huge musth elephant came, a man drove it off, and no one but him shall touch her friend's shoulders.
14.nuance: The friend puts herself in the scene (மாதரும் யானும்), so she speaks as witness to the rescue: her testimony is what makes the claim binding on the household. பருக்கை in line 2 is uncertain; the sense does not turn on it.

thinai_evidence.note: jackfruit hill, field platform and elephant are kurinji

15.reading: The friend tells the girl's kin that unless they receive the steadfast elders when they come and give her without wavering, not even the whole sea-girt world would be price enough for her unfailing beauty and her breasts.
15.nuance: The argument turns the bride price inside out: since nothing could buy her, she can only be given, and the giving is the rite with the suitor's elders (சான்றோர்) received at the door. கோடா / கோடாது is played twice, the kin must not swerve, and her beauty does not.

thinai_evidence.note: the poem has no landscape; its pressure for the wedding follows the kurinji sequence

16.reading: The man says he will not go until she of the wet hair fragrant with fresh naagam flowers grants him her ornamented breast; he has said 'her ornamented breast': is there a second way? And he has taken his stand on the palmyra horse in the middle of the street.
16.nuance: The repeated பூண் ஆகம் makes his demand a single, fixed word that he will not trade; 'is there a second?' closes off any other remedy, so mounting the madal in the street is the only one left.

thinai_evidence.note: the madal threat belongs to the kurinji lover refused

links.note: Thinaimalai 1 gives the man's question to the girls about a wounded beast (ஏமரை); Thinaimozhi 8 gives the friend's answer that no wounded tusker came this way.
links.teaches: Put together the two short books make one exchange, and the question's lavish praise of the girls' faces next to the friend's flat denial shows each side treating the wounded animal as a cover: he courts through it, and she refuses through it.

links.note: In 1 the man asks after the arrow-struck deer; in 9 he tells his companion that the asking after a beast was a ruse (வஞ்சமே) and that he was the one taken.
links.teaches: The book places the pretext and the confession apart, so 9 tells the reader how to read 1: the hunter's question was never about game, and the hunter who set out to deceive came back captured.

links.note: Ainthinai 14 has the friend say the man came 'like those who ask after a beast' (மாவினவு வார்போல) with something else to ask; Thinaimalai 9 has the man himself call his asking after a beast deceit.
links.teaches: The ruse is seen through from both sides, the friend naming it as a likeness and the hero confessing it as a trick, which shows the beast question as a convention both parties knew and played along with rather than a deception that worked.

links.note: In Akananuru 388 the girl, in private, mocks the diviner whose god is said to have caused her sickness; in Thinaimalai 12 the friend tells the household to send the velan away, free the kid and recognise the man who saved her from the flood.
links.teaches: The long poem stops at the girl's private scorn for the rite, and the short one shows the next move, so the pair shows mockery of the velan turning into the friend's disclosure to the family, where dismissing the diviner and naming the rescuer are one act.

links.note: 12 says the girl will give her shoulders only to the man who swam the flood and set her on the bank; 14 says no one but the man who drove off the elephant shall touch her friend's shoulders. Both use the same 'except him, no one' formula.
links.teaches: The same exclusive formula is fitted to two different rescues, flood and elephant, which shows that the rescue is an interchangeable warrant and that what the friend really presents to the household is the girl's choice, already made.

links.note: 2 tells of the man who dressed the girl's hair with flowers and drove off the musth elephant from the platform; 14 tells of the elephant driven off and concludes that no one but him shall touch her shoulders.
links.teaches: Read in order, 2 lays out the evidence (the flowers in her hair, the rescue) and 14 draws the verdict, so the disclosure to the household is built like a case: first the facts, then the right those facts give him.

links.note: Kural 1131 says that for those who suffer in love there is no safeguard and strength but the palmyra horse; in Thinaimalai 16 the man stands on the madal in the street and will not leave until she grants him her breast.
links.teaches: The couplet names the madal as the lover's only strength in general terms, and the quatrain shows what that strength is in use: a public siege in the street with a single stated condition and no second way, so the 'safeguard' is pressure on her household, not comfort for him.

links.note: Kural 1085 has the man at first sight find in her look Death, an eye and a doe; Thinaimalai 8 has the man at the fields find Kaman's arrows, five twice over, in the girl's two eyes.
links.teaches: Both men read a killing power in the first look, but the Kural names it Death while the field poem gives it to the love god and counts the arrows, which shows the same wound drawn once as mortal danger and once as a wound meant to be healed in union.

links.note: In Natrinai 300 a suitor sets a great chariot at the gate as the price of the girl's bangles (சிறு வளை விலை); in Thinaimalai 15 the friend says no price, not the sea-girt world, could buy the girl, and she must be given to the elders who come for her.
links.teaches: Natrinai shows a bride price actually offered, and Thinaimalai answers the practice: by declaring her beyond any price the friend moves the marriage from purchase to gift, so the only claim the household should honour is the formal coming of the suitor's elders.

links.note: Akananuru 18 says that if the man suffers harm on the night ford even once, her friend will not live after it, and asks him to come by day; Thinaimalai 7 says that if he comes by night the daughter of the hill lord will not live.
links.teaches: Thinaimalai's flat 'she will not live' is explained by Akananuru 18: her life hangs on his safety on the path, so forbidding the night visit protects her through him, and the long poem's offer of a daytime meeting shows what the short ban leaves for him to infer.

links.note: Thinaimozhi 2 says the guarding of the millet fields has ended and asks whether his coming will now be hard; Thinaimalai 5 says the millet has ripened like the fruit of past deeds and that this parts them.
links.teaches: Thinaimozhi gives the harvest as a fact of the field, and Thinaimalai frames the same harvest as the ripening of deeds into their fruit, which turns the end of the meetings from a farming date into something like fate, and so adds weight to the push for marriage.

source_issues: 1-16: the core records carry no colophon thurai, so thurai_akam speaker, addressee and stage are inferred from the poems and occasion.words is null throughout.

13 lines 3-4: நாதும் (twice) is probably நாகும் / நாகம் (snake; with கைவாய், elephant); the reading of both lines depends on it.
4 line 2: ஆடா அடகினும் and line 3 கலம்புக்க are unclear; the reading of the verse turns on them.
